items.title: Alex Kendrick’s Blunt Message to Christians
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Alex Kendrick is gearing up for a fascinating theatrical expedition as he and his brother, Stephen, prepare to return to their roots in a truly unique way.

In fact, the brothers are set to release, “Flywheel: Ignition of the Soul,” on Oct. 16, a remake of their popular 2003 movie, “Flywheel.”

“‘Flywheel’ was our very first movie shot in standard definition, not even high definition, over 20 years ago,” Alex Kendrick recently told CBN News. “And [I] kind of fell on my face thinking I could make a good feature film, and it turned out to be pretty low production quality.”

In fact, he said, he almost didn’t release the movie as he didn’t realize at the time how difficult filmmaking can be. Ultimately, though, the brothers proceeded — and the rest is history.

“The only thing I did right was beg God to use it,” Kendrick said. “And my brother Stephen helping me and saying, ‘We need to pray Ephesians 3:20 — that God would do exceedingly abundantly more than we could ask or imagine. So that’s the only thing we did right.”

Despite being green filmmakers at the time, the Kendricks were shocked to see how God showed up. “Flywheel” sold 1.3 million DVDs and had a massive response from audiences — much larger than they could have ever imagined.

“People said once they got over the production quality, like 10 minutes into it, then they were moved by the story, and they would come back and say, ‘I saw a version of myself on the screen,'” Kendrick said. “And the the Lord did what only the Lord can do by touching their hearts, and so we’ve always wanted to remake that, and higher quality over the years.”

That idea started coming to fruition two years ago, when the Kendricks were in Brazil releasing, “The Forge,” another faith-based film. The duo took some young Christian filmmakers through a boot camp and, through that experience and through prayer, the idea was birthed to work with teams there to remake, “Flywheel.”

“The Lord opened the door for us to remake, ‘Flywheel,'” he said. “We instantly got the funding, the support, the distribution, so we reshot it in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in Portuguese, and had wonderful cast and crew that love the Lord help us make it, and so it’s made in their culture, their language. They’re so thrilled about it.”

Kendrick said pre-screenings of the film have left audiences crying and cheering. The movie has now been dubbed for Americans audiences into English. Regardless of the language in which the film is viewed, Kendrick believes audiences will love it.

“This movie that talks about lordship and is now modernized [and] is coming out in theaters Oct. 16,” he said. “Can’t wait to see what the Lord does with this one.”

Kendrick believes this movie is releasing at the right cultural moment, with the main character working as a successful used car salesman when he goes through a very dark time in his life. This man realizes he needs more than his own logic to navigate it all, seeking help in marriage, fatherhood — and more. It’s his newfound faith in Jesus that changes everything.

“We do not need more lukewarm Christians,” Kendrick said. “What we need is Christians who are sold out and truly followers of Jesus Christ.”

He continued, “When people see the life of a Christian, what they don’t need to see is half-hearted commitment to our Savior, and half-hearted integrity. They need to see someone who lives for a higher purpose, because we serve an almighty God and that the way we live bears fruit of that relationship.”

Kendrick is hoping — much like the first “Flywheel” — people see themselves on the screen and confront spiritual issues in their own lives.

items.title: PRAY: 24-Year-Old Youth Pastor Dies Running Portland Marathon
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: A youth pastor died after rounding one of the miles of the Portland Marathon on Sunday. Treyton “Trey” Lara, 24, […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A youth pastor died after rounding one of the miles of the Portland Marathon on Sunday.

Treyton “Trey” Lara, 24, reportedly collapsed just before mile 20 of the marathon, right after slowing down briefly to give his wife, Audrey Shin-Lara, a kiss between miles 18 and 19.

“He ran over, was able to give me a kiss, was smiling, and then ran off,” she told local Portland news outlet KGW-TV. “He looked good. And then so I drove off to the finish line, where the rest of our family and friends were going to watch him finish.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Trey Lara (@treytonlara)

Audrey, 24, had been moving with him the entire race. She first stopped to cheer him on at mile 10, then mile 14, then mile 18, and was headed to the end to celebrate all together.

The now-grieving wife said Trey had been training for months and showed no signs of distress of health issues at all, describing running as something her husband did to “relax and release.”

Soon after loading into the car to head to the finish line, Audrey said her mother-in-law called her, telling her Trey had collapsed around mile 20 and that first responders were performing CPR on him. He was transported to a nearby hospital but, by that point, doctors said it was too late.

“We’re all still in a little bit of shock,” said Audrey. “We tried going to bed and we’re like, ‘We’re gonna wake up and it’ll be a really bad dream. And he’ll be right there.'”

While they were married for just under five years, Audrey told reporters they first met one another at 12 years old. She called her late husband “one of one.”

“We met at a summer camp,” she remembered. “He saw me, and I guess he told his friends and even his best friend’s mom, he said, ‘That’s the girl I’m going to marry.’ And I didn’t actually believe it, but now I want to believe it.”

Camp was clearly a major theme in the Laras’ lives.

The couple had just launched a youth summer camp of their own, Camp Genesis, this past summer.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Trey Lara (@treytonlara)

“[I]t was just this dream that he had,” Audrey said of the nascent ministry. “He was the biggest dreamer but it wasn’t just like, ‘I’m going to do this,’ but he’s like, ‘I will do this,’ and we got it done.”

Loved ones set up a GoFundMe campaign to raise money as the family walks through this difficult time. The account describes Trey as a man whose “confidence was unshakable and his faith unwavering.”

“His faith was his defining feature,” it states. “It has spoken the loudest to those who knew him, whether they spent years with him, months with him, or even just a single day. They recognized that Trey’s faith and passion for advancing the Kingdom of God were at the center of his life.”

“He was devoted to his family and friends,” it continues. “He loved his wife, Audrey, from the moment he met her. His sisters, Jaylah and Sylvia, had the best role model in an older brother, and his parents, Omar and Misty, had the most devoted son. The man Trey became directly reflected the values they instilled in him.”

The purpose of the campaign, it notes, is to provide for Audrey’s immediate needs in the wake of her husband’s death.

Please pray for the Laras and all those impacted by this loss.

items.title: It’s Not Just You: Instagram Has Been Pushing Creed’s ‘Higher’ on Everyone’s Stories But Doesn’t Know Why
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: If you posted a photo of your dog, a dinner plate or a caesar salad to your Instagram Story lately and the app suggested Creed’s “Higher” to go with it, you weren’t imagining things. A company spokesperson told CNN the team “looked into this and found that this song is being recommended to mor
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

If you posted a photo of your dog, a dinner plate or a caesar salad to your Instagram Story lately and the app suggested Creed’s “Higher” to go with it, you weren’t imagining things. A company spokesperson told CNN the team “looked into this and found that this song is being recommended to more people than intended.” The company is still investigating, she said, and its engineering team is working on a fix.

Her first response, when she was asked about it, was a little less official: “That song is always recommended to me too!”

Users have been noticing for weeks. “I can’t prove it but pretty sure Creed is paying META to suggest their song ‘Higher’ on all Instagram Stories,” one person wrote on X in August. In September, another posted that they had found out it was happening to other people and said, “I feel like I’m uncovering a big conspiracy.” A third said Instagram “almost had me this time” with a caesar salad.

Instagram is supposed to pick songs the same way it recommends everything else, weighing signals like which songs you have used before and what is in the photo or video you have selected. Nothing about a cat or a plate of pasta should point to a 1999 rock radio staple.

Pamela Ross, a communications specialist, said it happened every time she posted anything to her Story, “like a dinner plate or my cat or whatever.” She told CNN, “I’m not following Creed, I’m not listening to Creed. Like what millennial was in charge of this decision?”

Instagram’s answer is that nobody was. It was a mistake, and it is being fixed.

Creed is not the only song people have been side-eyeing. Some users also flagged Soulja Boy’s “Turn My Swag On” for showing up more often than seemed plausible. Instagram says that one is working as designed: “The Soulja Boy song being recommended is not a bug, and it is actually popular on IG!”

So the Soulja Boy suggestions reflect real demand, and the Creed suggestions were a mistake. If your Story has spent the past few weeks trying to go “Higher,” that was Instagram’s doing, and nothing about your taste put it there.

items.title: John Prine’s Beatific Vision
items.author: Eric Cyr
items.summary:
Eric Cyr

Prine reminds us that there is joy that fulfills beyond what we can imagine or try to substitute on earth—joy in the fullness of reunion and communion with God.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Eric Cyr

October 10 this year marks the 80th birthday of one of America’s greatest wordsmiths, the late John Prine. When Prine came to Duluth, Minnesota, in the summer of 2019, I almost didn’t go to see him. I had listened to him a little bit in the past on my dad’s cassette of Prime Prine and once or twice to the 2018 album The Tree of Forgiveness that he was touring behind, but I had never gotten too deep into his music and was on the fence about buying tickets. But sometimes you can encounter the same thing a half dozen times without being moved, and then the seventh time through, for whatever reason, you’re prepared to receive it for the first time. In the months preceding the concert, I gave Prine’s music a closer listen and realized what I had been missing out on; I got my tickets and went with my dad. Now, especially after Prine’s untimely death in 2020, going to that show remains one of my biggest near misses—an event I know I was this close to missing out on and am so grateful to have experienced.

Many books and analyses could be written about Prine and his songs, and I’m sure many have been, but I want to focus on one song on that 2018 album where Prine gives his dream of the afterlife. The song “When I Get to Heaven” is the last track on the album, and you can watch and listen to an especially moving live performance recorded at the House of Strombo.

To preface, any theology that comes up in Prine’s work has never been strong, in any orthodox or even consistently thought-through sense. I don’t know that he ever gave theology as a field of knowledge or truth much thought. And while his album The Missing Years earned him a Grammy in 1991, Prine’s account of Jesus’s “missing years” leaves much historically and theologically to be desired. Still, writer Andrew Tolkmith has pointed out that in spite of Prine being no theologian or proponent of the Church, his music points toward a longing for redemption and hope. And, despite his depiction of heaven looking very different on the surface from biblical or theological descriptions, some beautiful truths that lie at the heart of all human longing break through in Prine’s “vision” of heaven.

After a flourish of strings that sounds like cartoon angels plucking their golden harps, Prine begins by speaking,

When I get to heaven, I’m gonna shake God’s hand
And thank Him for more blessings than one man can stand.

In this opening line, Prine emphasizes the incredible blessings of life. He expresses thanks for the particular blessings of his own life, but we know that each one of us has also received our own blessings and the pure gift that is life itself. It would be easy for Prine or any of us to complain about all the things that are wrong in the world, all the things that have not gone the way we wanted, all the things we haven’t received or that we think are unfair. The grotesque pleasure of complaint is an all too human tendency. But all is a gift, and Prine acknowledges that we ought first to recognize the gift and blessings that precede and overpower anything we could complain about.

Each verse of “When I Get to Heaven” is spoken instead of sung by Prine, with soft guitar chords underneath. Bare and stripped down, the verses give us the simplified music of the earthly pilgrim in exile, looking and longing heavenward. As the song shifts into the chorus, the music and lyrics complete the movement toward heaven, from the sojourn to the destination. Prine sings accompanied by a chorus of voices, jangling piano, and buzzing kazoos in a joyful outburst. Here, Prine sings,

And then I’m gonna get a cocktail, vodka and ginger ale
Yeah, I’m gonna smoke a cigarette that’s nine miles long
I’m gonna kiss that pretty girl on the Tilt-A-Whirl
’Cause this old man is goin’ to town.

As I mentioned earlier, this is not the description of the heavenly Jerusalem you will find in your Bible, and it is, admittedly, open to critique. For instance, is heaven really no more than a place where we can do the things that are bad for us and “sin taxed” on earth? But I don’t think that is fair to Prine’s intent, and the lyrics go beyond that surface-level criticism.

For one, we do experience a sense of longing on earth that is only fulfilled in heaven that Prine expresses here in his own way. In the performance at the House of Strombo, Prine says he smoked a pack a day for thirty-five years until he got cancer and his doctor convinced him to quit. For him, smoking a cigarette was a pleasure on earth that also carried with it (as it does for anyone) a cost and a risk. Forgive me if this is taking a leap too far, but all pleasures on earth are imperfect; they carry with them the risk of overindulgence, intemperance, and some kind of earthly price. Prine, in his own way, describes the desire to eat without cost and to be filled without price. At the heart of this heavenly vision is the desire to be fulfilled. Certainly the things he pictures himself being fulfilled by are not the highest goods or the goods we imagine will be in heaven, but the heart of his vision speaks to that longing which cannot be fulfilled on earth.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

The same can be said in a different sense about the third line of the chorus. On earth, human and specifically romantic relationships are a great good—an important way we are called to imitate God and a preparation for the union of heaven. Yet we so often distort and pervert what that relationship is supposed to be. The innocent, nostalgic image of kissing “that pretty girl on the Tilt-A-Whirl” speaks to a desire for the redemption of romantic relationships, a rectifying of distorted lust back to a chastened love. In Prine’s vision, things that are fallen on earth are turned to a perfected version in heaven. Again, some listeners could hear this as a problem—heaven as the bad things on earth being made not bad anymore, heaven as sin without the consequences. But that doesn’t feel like Prine’s point for several reasons, in part because we know that God really does turn all things to the good. Vodka, cigarettes, kissing a pretty girl: none of these are evil or immoral in themselves, and there’s a recognition that what we overindulge in or twist into sin in our fallen state on earth are meant for good, for blessing, which God can redeem in the end.

Both lyrically and musically, the aspect of “When I Get to Heaven” that I find most moving is the shift from the sincere longing of the verse, of the earthly pilgrim, to the overwhelming sense of joy in the chorus. We feel this most strongly in the third verse, where Prine says,

And then I’m gonna go find my mom and dad and good old brother Doug
Why, I bet him and cousin Jackie are still cuttin’ up a rug
I wanna see all my mama’s sisters ’cause that’s where all the love starts
I miss them all like crazy, bless their little hearts.

The sense of longing for union and communion is so strong here, and Prine’s gravel, world-worn voice gives a sense that he knows he’s nearly there, that his heart is halfway to this reunion. After these lines, the song breaks into its final raucous chorus and emphasizes what I think is most powerful in Prine’s image of heaven: the joyful sense of play.

What does Prine lean into when he thinks about heaven? Communion, laughter, the voice of a child, a chorus of voices singing in harmony, buzzing kazoos, fun—this sense of play is something that isn’t always emphasized when we think about heaven but is something that I think helps us in a more complete vision of heaven. In God, we find peace and communion but also ebullience, laughter, joy, and play; when we think of heaven as only somber, our human experience of somberness is disloyal to the actual promise of heaven. I don’t mean to say that heaven is supercilious or frivolous, but play and fun are good and therefore belong as part of the fullness of heaven in some way that we don’t yet fully comprehend. In spite of himself, Prine reminds us that there is joy in the heavenly kingdom, joy that fulfills beyond what we can imagine or try to substitute on earth, joy in the fullness of reunion and communion with God. And I pray wholeheartedly that when (and if) I get to heaven, I’ll be able to sing a joyful chorus with John Prine.

items.title: Saturday, October 10, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus transforms a woman’s blessing of his mother into a blessing of those who obey God’s word.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 3:22-29

But the scripture has imprisoned all things under the power of sin, so that what was promised through faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.

Now before faith came, we were imprisoned and guarded under the law until faith would be revealed. Therefore the law was our disciplinarian until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer subject to a disciplinarian, for in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith. As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. There is no longer Jew or Greek, there is no longer slave or free, there is no longer male and female; for all of you are one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.

Psalm
Psalm 105:2-3, 4-5, 6-7

Sing to him, sing praises to him;
    tell of all his wonderful works.
Glory in his holy name;
    let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice.
Seek the Lord and his strength;
    seek his presence continually.
Remember the wonderful works he has done,
    his miracles, and the judgments he has uttered,
O offspring of his servant Abraham,
    children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
He is the Lord our God;
    his judgments are in all the earth.

Gospel Reading
Luke 11:27-28

While he was saying this, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!” But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus transforms a woman’s blessing of his mother into a blessing of those who obey God’s word. Jesus turned upside down many of the social conventions of his time because he was so concerned with placing the instantiation of the kingdom of God first in the minds of his followers.

Among first-century Jews, the family was of paramount importance. An enthusiastic disciple of Jesus took this for granted when she shouted out, “Blessed is the womb that carried you and the breasts at which you nursed.” But Jesus dramatically relativizes the family in responding, “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and observe it.”

He is insisting that the new community of the kingdom is more important than even the most revered social system. When we give the family a disproportionate importance, it becomes—in short order—dysfunctional.

Another time, a prospective disciple said that he was willing to follow Jesus but first begged permission to bury his father. But Jesus, having none of it, responded in a manner that undoubtedly scandalized him: “Let the dead bury their dead.” Once again, he was insisting that God’s kingdom is of paramount importance.
